back2basics.text: Plug-and-play industrial parks are pre-developed industrial areas where essential infrastructure like roads, power, water, and utilities are provided in advance. They often include streamlined regulatory approvals through single-window systems, allowing industries to start operations faster and at lower initial cost. This model supports faster industrial growth by reducing entry barriers and improving ease of doing business.

Consider the following statements about the BHAVYA initiative:

body.label: Scheme overview
body.text: BHAVYA is a ₹33,660 crore initiative to develop 100 plug-and-play industrial parks across India, providing modern infrastructure, reliable services, and faster approvals to reduce setup time for new industries.

body.label: Key objectives
body.text: The scheme aims to attract investment, support MSMEs, strengthen supply chains, create jobs, and drive industrial growth across regions.

body.label: Implementation partners
body.text: BHAVYA is implemented in partnership with States and private developers, emphasizing ease of doing business through streamlined approvals and single-window systems.

sections.heading: What is the BHAVYA initiative and its objectives?

body.label: Pre-2020 phase
body.text: The focus was on industrial estates and Special Economic Zones (SEZs) providing land, infrastructure, and fiscal incentives; by February 2026, India had 370 notified SEZs attracting ₹7.82 lakh crore investment and generating over 31.7 lakh jobs.

body.label: National Industrial Corridor Development Programme
body.text: NICDP expanded from land provision to integrated manufacturing zones with utilities, logistics, and urban services, creating smart industrial cities like Dholera SIR.

body.label: Plug-and-play model
body.text: BHAVYA represents the nationwide rollout of plug-and-play parks, building on sector-specific parks and cluster models introduced in Budget 2026-27.

sections.heading: How has India's manufacturing policy evolved to BHAVYA?

body.label: Infrastructure components
body.text: Financial assistance up to ₹1 crore per acre supports internal roads, power, water, drainage, effluent treatment, ICT-enabled administration, and underground utility corridors for maintenance.

body.label: Facilities for industries and workers
body.text: Parks include ready-built factory sheds, built-to-suit units, testing facilities, warehousing, worker housing, healthcare, skill development centers, and social amenities.

body.label: Connectivity and integration
body.text: Up to 25% of funding supports external infrastructure like roads, rail, and last-mile logistics to ensure seamless integration with transport networks.

body.label: Implementation and selection
body.text: The scheme spans FY2026–27 to FY2031–32; initially, up to 50 parks will be selected through challenge mode based on project readiness, land availability, and industrial potential.

sections.heading: What are the features and benefits of plug-and-play industrial parks under BHAVYA?

body.label: Manufacturing sector growth
body.text: India's manufacturing contributes about 16–17% of GDP and employs over 27 million workers; the National Manufacturing Mission targets raising this to 25% by 2035.

body.label: Shift to technology-intensive industries
body.text: Medium- and high-technology industries now account for 46.3% of manufacturing value addition, reflecting a move towards higher-value manufacturing.

body.label: Reducing entry barriers
body.text: Plug-and-play parks reduce time and cost for new units by providing essential infrastructure and streamlined approvals before operations begin.

body.label: Global supply chain relevance
body.text: Diversifying global supply chains increase demand for well-connected, infrastructure-ready industrial locations, which BHAVYA aims to provide.

sections.heading: Why does BHAVYA matter for India's manufacturing sector?

back2basics.concept: Right to Protest and Public Space Regulation
back2basics.text: The right to protest is a fundamental democratic right allowing citizens to express dissent publicly. Governments regulate protests to balance public order and safety with civil liberties. Designated protest sites are official locations where demonstrations can be held legally, ensuring order while allowing public expression.

This incident highlights ongoing tensions over the regulation of protest sites and the right to demonstrate in India's capital, a key issue for civil liberties and governance.

back2basics.text: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) refers to investment from a foreign entity into a domestic company, allowing ownership or control. In banking, FDI can bring capital, technology, and management expertise, but is regulated to protect financial stability. The Reserve Bank of India oversees banks, including those with foreign investment, ensuring prudential norms and depositor protection.

body.label: Poor financial health
body.text: IDBI Bank faced poor financial health requiring repeated capital infusion by the Government of India and LIC, and was placed under RBI's Prompt Corrective Action framework in 2017 due to high non-performing assets.

body.label: Improvement and restructuring
body.text: RBI lifted restrictions in 2021 after financial improvements, leading to the Cabinet's approval of strategic restructuring involving sale of 60.72% equity to a strategic buyer.

sections.heading: What is the background and reason for the IDBI Bank sale?

body.label: Competitive bidding
body.text: A two-stage competitive bidding process was conducted with eligibility criteria including RBI's 'Fit and Proper' assessment and security clearance by the Ministry of Home Affairs.

body.label: Qualified bidders
body.text: Out of five initial parties, four qualified and two submitted techno-financial bids; Fairfax Financial Holdings (through M/s 10955230 Canada Inc.) was selected as the strategic buyer.

body.label: Purchase consideration
body.text: The approved purchase consideration was ₹52,878.0806181 crore for acquiring 60.72% stake, split equally between the Government of India (30.48%) and LIC (30.24%).

sections.heading: How was the sale process conducted and who is the buyer?

body.label: Valuation methods
body.text: Two independent professional agencies used the Market Multiple Method and Asset Valuation Method based on March 31, 2026 accounts to determine fair market and net asset values.

body.label: Benchmark price
body.text: The average of the two valuations, ₹75.99 per share, served as the benchmark price; the winning bid of ₹81 per share was above this benchmark and deemed reasonable.

body.label: Stock price role
body.text: Volatile stock market prices were disregarded as they misaligned with intrinsic value; valuation relied on accounting-based methods.

sections.heading: How was the valuation of IDBI Bank determined?

body.label: Largest FDI in financial sector
body.text: This transaction is the largest foreign direct investment in India's financial sector, expected to boost investor confidence and economic reforms.

body.label: Post-privatization benefits
body.text: IDBI Bank is expected to generate funds without government assistance, with Fairfax bringing private capital, technology, and management practices to enhance competitiveness.

body.label: Residual shareholding
body.text: The Government of India retains 15% and LIC retains 19% residual stakes, with plans for minority stake sales through open market mechanisms.

body.label: Regulatory oversight
body.text: RBI continues full regulatory and prudential supervision; depositor interests and priority sector lending norms remain unaffected.

sections.heading: What are the implications of this transaction for the banking sector and economy?

back2basics.text: Electricity demand varies daily and seasonally, requiring careful balancing with supply to avoid outages. States procure power from various sources including thermal, gas, and renewable energy. When local generation is insufficient, states may buy power from other sources, sometimes at higher costs, to maintain supply reliability. Managing peak demand, forecasting shortages, and integrating renewables are key challenges in power sector management.

back2basics.text: A trade deficit occurs when a country imports more goods and services than it exports, resulting in a negative balance of trade. It indicates that more money is leaving the country to pay for imports than is coming in from exports. Persistent trade deficits can affect a country’s currency value, foreign exchange reserves, and economic policy decisions.

back2basics.concept: Crop Residue Management and Environmental Impact
back2basics.text: Crop residue or stubble is the leftover plant material after harvesting crops like paddy. Burning stubble releases harmful pollutants causing air pollution and damages soil health by destroying nutrients and beneficial organisms. Crop residue management involves alternative uses such as converting stubble into organic manure, biofuels, or fodder, which helps protect the environment and supports sustainable agriculture.

2026-10-14-pm-7c1ad78619.deck: Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan and Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav held a high-level meeting on October 13, 2026, to review and accelerate stubble management efforts during the paddy harvesting season. This is important for UPSC aspirants as it highlights government strategies to curb stubble burning, a major environmental and agricultural challenge.

body.text: Ministers directed district collectors to take immediate ground-level action to prevent stubble burning, emphasizing that very little time remains between harvesting and sowing of rabi crops.

back2basics.concept: Audit and accountability in cooperative societies
back2basics.text: Cooperative societies are member-owned organizations that require transparent financial and governance practices to protect members' interests. Audits are independent examinations of financial records and compliance to ensure accuracy and accountability. A statutory audit framework mandates uniform reporting standards and oversight mechanisms to detect irregularities and enforce good governance.

body.label: MSCARO, 2026 introduction
body.text: The Multi-State Co-operative Societies (Auditor’s Report) Order, 2026 (MSCARO, 2026) introduces a uniform, structured, and risk-based statutory audit reporting framework for Multi-State Cooperative Societies.

body.label: Purpose of the framework
body.text: It aims to strengthen transparency, accountability, financial discipline, and good governance while safeguarding members’ funds.

body.label: Audit reporting format
body.text: Auditors must report on financial, administrative, governance, and statutory compliance parameters using a standardized format with clear Yes/No responses and remarks.

body.label: Risk-based supervision
body.text: The framework enables risk-based regulatory supervision by the Central Registrar of Cooperative Societies (CRCS) to identify societies with higher financial or governance risks for focused inspections.

sections.heading: What is the new audit reporting framework for Multi-State Cooperative Societies?

body.label: Early detection of financial stress
body.text: Systematic reporting of Non-Performing Assets, overdue loans, liquidity, deposits, advances, and defaults helps identify financial vulnerabilities early for timely remedial action.

body.label: Protection of members’ funds
body.text: Independent verification of investments, fund utilization, share capital, membership records, and statutory approvals reinforces financial integrity and members’ confidence.

body.label: Good governance measures
body.text: The framework mandates scrutiny of board composition, director eligibility, meeting conduct, statutory committees, and related-party transactions to promote transparency and democratic functioning.

body.label: Technology-enabled oversight
body.text: Integration with the CRCS Portal allows automated scrutiny, risk scoring, AI analytics, and regulatory dashboards for efficient monitoring and evidence-based interventions.

body.label: Compliance with cybersecurity and anti-money laundering
body.text: Audit-level verification includes cybersecurity safeguards and compliance with the Prevention of Money Laundering Act to mitigate financial irregularities and cyber risks.

sections.heading: Why does the new framework matter for governance and accountability?

body.label: Phased implementation
body.text: The framework is being implemented in phases, starting with larger societies crossing ₹1,000 crore in financial parameters, giving smaller societies more time to comply.

body.label: Long-term extension
body.text: Eventually, MSCARO, 2026 will apply to all Multi-State Cooperative Societies exceeding ₹50 crore in relevant financial parameters.

sections.heading: How is the framework being implemented and what are its future plans?
